summary: This RFC specifies how to wrap IP datagrams for sending over an Experimental Ethernet, an early form of Ethernet. It gives the basic framing so that IP hosts on the same cable can exchange packets.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how to carry IP datagrams over the 3-megabit Experimental Ethernet. It specifies the frame type, address mapping, packet-size limit, and rules for an optional alternate format.

subtitle: Defines how IP datagrams are carried in frames on the 3-megabit Experimental Ethernet.

tldr.problem: Hosts on Experimental Ethernet need a shared way to place IP datagrams in Ethernet frames and map Internet addresses to local addresses.
tldr.mechanism: Frames use type value 513, carry the IP header and data, and map the host part's last eight bits to the Ethernet address as the recommended method.
tldr.outcome: The RFC sets a maximum IP datagram length of 1536 octets for this network and describes optional trailer encapsulation for systems that know the receiver supports it.

today: RFC 895 is listed as an Internet Standard in the unit metadata. It covers Experimental Ethernet; RFC 894 describes the 10-megabit Ethernet method.

sections.title: Experimental Ethernet Only
sections.content: The memo applies to Experimental Ethernet, which runs at 3 megabits per second and uses 8-bit addresses. The procedure for the 10-megabit Ethernet with 48-bit addresses is described separately in RFC 894.
sections.plainLanguage: This method is for the slower Experimental Ethernet with short addresses. The RFC points to a separate standard for the 10-megabit Ethernet.

sections.title: Ethernet Frame Format
sections.content:
An IP datagram is sent in a standard Experimental Ethernet frame. The frame type field must be 513 (1001 octal), and its data field contains the IP header followed by the IP data.

If padding is needed to reach the minimum frame size, it is not part of the IP packet and is not included in the IP total-length field. The maximum IP datagram length is 1536 octets; gateways must accept full-length packets and fragment them if necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The type value tells the receiver that the frame contains IP. The frame may include padding, but the padding is not counted as part of the IP datagram.

sections.title: Mapping Internet and Ethernet Addresses
sections.content: The recommended mapping uses the last 8 bits of the host-number part of the 32-bit Internet address as the 8-bit Experimental Ethernet address. The broadcast Internet address, whose host part is all binary ones, maps to Ethernet address zero.
sections.plainLanguage: A host's short Ethernet address comes from the last part of its Internet address. Broadcast traffic uses Ethernet address zero.

sections.title: Optional Trailer Format and Byte Order
sections.content:
Some systems may use a trailer encapsulation format between hosts on the same Ethernet. No host is required to support it, and a sender should use it only when it knows the recipient can interpret it.

The IP datagram is transmitted as a sequence of 8-bit bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The alternate trailer format is optional and must only be sent to a host known to support it. Otherwise, hosts use the standard frame method.
